title: Sharpest ever view of the Andromeda Galaxy
caption: The Andromeda Galaxy (M31), imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: Andromeda Galaxy, M 31, Messier 31 · constellation Andromeda · about 2 million light-years away (source figure)
credit: NASA, ESA, J. Dalcanton (University of Washington, USA), B. F. Williams (University of Washington, USA), L. C. Johnson (University of Washington, USA), the PHAT team, and R. Gendler.

recognition.text: Ranked #91 on ESA/Hubble’s published “Top 100 Images” list (an institutional selection, not an audience score).

story: More than 100 million stars, along with thousands of star clusters, crowd this Hubble view of the Andromeda galaxy, also known as M31. It covers a section of the galaxy's flat, pancake-shaped disc reaching across more than 40 000 light-years.

The full image was the largest and sharpest ever made of Andromeda, and the biggest Hubble image ever released. Even this cropped version holds 1.5 billion pixels. Showing the whole picture at full resolution would take more than 600 HD television screens, so it is best explored with a zoom tool.

Andromeda is a spiral galaxy about 2 million light-years away, in the constellation that shares its name. Because it is so close, Hubble can separate individual stars across a whole stretch of its disc, rather than just the blended glow seen in more distant galaxies. That is how a single picture can show more than 100 million stars.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (57.98 x 18.54 arcminutes) and distance (2 million light years), the frame spans roughly 34,000 × 11,000 light-years. Its light set out about 2 million years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys observed through a blue filter and a near-infrared filter. The color mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: The near-infrared filter records light we cannot see, and Hubble separates stars that would blur together for the eye.
